terms.short: India's largest stock exchange
terms.definition: The National Stock Exchange of India, based in Mumbai. It is India's largest exchange by trading volume and runs the Nifty indices.
examples: Most of the volume in this stock is on NSE.
The desk routes most orders to NSE because that's where the depth is.
The client asked whether to buy on NSE or BSE; for a large stock the price is nearly the same.
terms.fill: The Nifty 50 index is run by the ____'s index arm.
wrong: India's securities market regulator
The older Mumbai exchange that runs the Sensex
India's central bank

terms.short: Asia's oldest exchange; runs the Sensex
terms.definition: BSE Ltd, formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange, founded in 1875 and the oldest stock exchange in Asia. Its flagship index is the Sensex.
examples: The stock is listed only on BSE, so liquidity is thin.
BSE won a much bigger share of options trading once its Sensex weekly contracts took off.
Risk checks the price on both NSE and BSE before marking a thinly traded stock.
terms.fill: The Sensex is the flagship index of the ____.
wrong: India's largest exchange by trading volume
The regulator of mutual funds
An exchange for commodities only

terms.short: Where shares themselves trade
terms.definition: The part of an exchange where shares themselves are bought and sold, for delivery or intraday, as opposed to the derivatives (F&O) segment.
examples: Cash market volumes are a fraction of F&O volumes.
The desk buys the shares in the cash segment and sells futures against them to lock in the basis.
The client only trades the cash segment; she doesn't touch futures or options.
terms.fill: Buying shares to hold for the long term happens in the ____, not in F&O.
wrong: The segment for currency trading
Trading paid for with physical cash
The segment for government bonds

terms.short: Futures and options segment
terms.definition: Futures and options: the derivatives segment of an exchange, where contracts on indices and stocks are traded.
examples: SEBI tightened F&O rules to cut retail losses.
Risk asked how much of the desk's loss came from F&O and how much from cash positions.
The client wants to start trading F&O, so the broker first asks for proof of income.
terms.fill: Contracts like Nifty futures and Bank Nifty options trade in the ____ segment.
wrong: Fixed income and other bonds
The segment where shares are delivered
A list of foreign-owned companies

terms.short: Founder or controlling shareholder
terms.definition: The founder, family or parent company that controls an Indian listed company, as declared in its filings.
examples: Promoters own 55% and haven't sold a share.
The analyst likes that the promoter has been buying shares in the open market.
Risk flags stocks where the promoter group has been selling steadily.
terms.fill: In India, the founding family that controls a listed company is called its ____.
wrong: A marketing firm hired for an IPO
A broker who recommends a stock
Any shareholder with more than 1%

terms.short: Shares available to the public
terms.definition: The shares freely available to trade, leaving out promoter holdings and other locked-in shares. Indices like the Nifty 50 weight companies by free-float market cap.
examples: With promoters holding 75%, the free float is small.
A small free float means a few large orders can move the price a long way.
The index weights the stock by its free float, so the promoter's 70% doesn't count.
terms.fill: A company whose promoters hold 90% of the shares has a very small ____.
wrong: The total number of shares issued
Shares that pay no dividend
Cash a company keeps outside its business

calcs.q: A company is worth ₹1 lakh crore and promoters hold 60%. Its free-float market cap is about?
calcs.why: Only the roughly 40% not held by promoters counts: 40% of ₹1 lakh crore.

terms.short: NSE index of 50 large companies
terms.definition: NSE's benchmark index of 50 large, liquid Indian companies, weighted by free-float market cap.
examples: Nifty closed up 1.2%, led by banks.
The client's index fund tracks the Nifty 50, so it holds the same 50 stocks.
Risk hedges the book with Nifty 50 futures because they are the most liquid.
terms.fill: The ____ tracks 50 large companies listed on NSE.
wrong: BSE's index of 30 large companies
An index of the biggest bank stocks
A list of the 50 most traded stocks of the day

terms.short: BSE index of 30 large companies
terms.definition: BSE's benchmark index of 30 large, well-established companies. It is India's oldest stock index, with a base year of 1978–79.
examples: The Sensex hit a record high today.
The evening news led with the Sensex falling 800 points.
The client asked why the Sensex and Nifty move almost together: they hold many of the same big companies.
terms.fill: The ____ is made up of 30 large companies listed on BSE.
wrong: NSE's index of 50 large companies
An index of mid-sized companies
India's volatility index

terms.short: NSE index of large bank stocks
terms.definition: NSE's index of the most liquid large Indian bank stocks. Its futures and options are among the most heavily traded contracts in India.
examples: Bank Nifty fell 2% as private lenders sold off.
The desk hedged its bank stocks with Bank Nifty futures before the RBI policy.
Risk watches Bank Nifty closely because banks are such a big part of the Nifty.
terms.fill: A trader who wants to bet on banks as a group can trade ____ futures.
wrong: A savings scheme run by banks
The RBI's list of approved banks
An index of all listed financial companies

terms.short: Top 100 companies by market cap
terms.definition: In India, the 100 largest listed companies by full market cap, under the classification that SEBI, the market regulator, sets for mutual funds. AMFI updates the list every six months.
examples: Large caps held up better than small caps in the sell-off.
The client's large cap fund can only hold the top 100 companies by market cap, such as Reliance and Infosys.
Risk prefers large cap stocks, the top 100 by market cap, for big positions because they can be sold quickly.
terms.fill: Under SEBI's rules, the 100 biggest companies by market cap are called ____ stocks.
wrong: Companies ranked 101st to 250th by market cap
Any company worth more than ₹1,000 crore
Only the companies in the Sensex

terms.short: Companies ranked 101 to 250
terms.definition: In India, companies ranked 101st to 250th by full market cap, under the same SEBI classification.
examples: Mid caps have rallied 40% this year.
The analyst thinks valuations of companies ranked 101 to 250, the mid cap segment, have run ahead of earnings.
The client's mid cap fund, which holds companies ranked 101 to 250, fell more than the Nifty in the correction.
terms.fill: A company ranked 180th by market cap is classed as a ____.
wrong: The 100 largest companies
Companies ranked 251st and below
Companies with medium debt levels

terms.short: Companies ranked 251 and below
terms.definition: In India, companies ranked 251st and below by full market cap. They tend to be more volatile and less liquid.
examples: Small caps were hit hardest when SEBI warned about froth.
Risk caps small cap holdings at 15% because they are hard to sell in a panic.
The client's small cap fund stopped taking lump sums for a while because the AMC worried about froth.
terms.fill: A company ranked 600th by market cap is a ____.
wrong: Companies ranked 101st to 250th
Companies with a share price below ₹100
Companies with fewer than 100 employees

aliases: Securities and Exchange Board of India
terms.short: India's securities market regulator
terms.definition: The Securities and Exchange Board of India, which regulates stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds and listed companies.
examples: SEBI's new F&O rules raised minimum contract sizes.
The compliance team reads every SEBI circular the day it comes out.
The client asked who keeps brokers honest; SEBI regulates them and can ban them.
terms.fill: Rules on IPO disclosures and insider trading are set by ____.
wrong: India's central bank
India's largest stock exchange
The company that runs mutual fund schemes

terms.short: India's central bank
terms.definition: The Reserve Bank of India, the central bank. It sets the repo rate, manages the rupee and regulates banks.
examples: The RBI held the repo rate unchanged.
The bond desk is waiting for the RBI policy at 10 am.
The client asked why the rupee jumped: traders think the RBI sold dollars.
terms.fill: The repo rate is set by the ____'s Monetary Policy Committee.
wrong: The stock market regulator
A government-owned bank for retail customers
The tax department of the finance ministry

terms.short: Firm that places your trades
terms.definition: A firm registered with SEBI and a member of an exchange, which places orders on the exchange for its clients.
examples: Discount brokers charge a flat fee per order.
The client is moving to a stockbroker with a better app and lower fees.
The analyst covers listed stockbroker firms, whose profits swing with F&O volumes.
terms.fill: Retail investors can't trade directly on NSE; they go through a ____.
wrong: The person who sets a stock's price
A bank that lends to companies
An analyst who rates stocks

terms.short: Holds securities electronically (NSDL, CDSL)
terms.definition: An institution that holds securities in electronic form and records who owns them. India has two: NSDL and CDSL.
examples: Your shares are recorded with CDSL through your broker.
If your broker shuts down, your shares are still safe at the depository.
The analyst covers CDSL, a listed depository whose income rises with new demat accounts.
terms.fill: Your shares are actually recorded with a ____ such as NSDL or CDSL.
wrong: The bank where brokers keep client money
The exchange where shares are listed
The company that settles trades and guarantees them

terms.short: Electronic account that holds your shares
terms.definition: An account that holds shares and other securities in electronic (dematerialised) form, opened through a depository participant.
examples: The shares will be credited to your demat account on listing day.
The client asked why her bonus shares hadn't shown up in her demat account yet.
India now has well over 15 crore demat accounts.
terms.fill: After you buy shares, they are held in your ____, not in your bank account.
wrong: A bank account for paying brokers
An account for trading derivatives only
A tax-saving account for investments

terms.short: Agent that runs your demat account
terms.definition: A depository participant: a broker or bank registered with a depository that opens and services your demat account.
examples: Your broker is also your DP, so it charges a DP fee when you sell.
The client paid a flat DP charge of about ₹15 for each stock that left her demat account, however many shares she sold.
To move shares to another broker, you ask your DP to transfer them.
terms.fill: When you sell shares from your demat account, your ____ charges a small fee for the debit.
wrong: A dividend-paying stock
The price at which an order is placed
The official who approves IPOs

terms.short: Broker account used to place orders
terms.definition: The account with your broker that you use to place buy and sell orders. It is linked to your demat account, which holds shares, and your bank account, which holds money.
examples: Add funds to the trading account before the market opens.
The client links her bank to her trading account so she can add money instantly.
The broker froze the trading account until the margin shortfall was paid.
terms.fill: You place orders through your ____, while the shares themselves sit in your demat account.
wrong: The account that holds your shares
An account at the exchange in your own name
A savings account with a higher interest rate

terms.short: Settles and guarantees trades
terms.definition: The entity that settles exchange trades and guarantees them, so neither side carries the other's default risk. For example, NSE Clearing for NSE and ICCL for BSE.
examples: The clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer.
If the other side of your trade defaults, the clearing corporation still pays you.
Risk keeps track of the margin the clearing corporation collects from every broker each day.
terms.fill: If the other side of your trade defaults, the ____ still makes sure you are paid.
wrong: The exchange's IT department
A bank that clears cheques
The body that approves new listings

terms.short: Settled one working day after the trade
terms.definition: Settlement one working day after the trade date: shares and money change hands the next working day. India moved fully to T+1 in January 2023.
examples: Buy on Monday and the shares reach your demat on Tuesday under T+1.
Under T+1, the money from Tuesday's sale reaches your account on Wednesday.
FPIs had to fund their trades faster when India moved to T+1 in 2023.
terms.fill: Under ____, a trade done on Thursday settles on Friday.
wrong: Trades settle the same day
Only one trade is allowed per day
Settlement two working days after the trade

terms.short: Tax on each trade in shares and F&O
terms.definition: Securities transaction tax: a tax on buying and selling securities on Indian exchanges, collected through your broker. Rates differ for delivery, intraday and F&O trades.
examples: Higher STT on options raised trading costs for active traders.
The client's options profit shrank because STT is charged on the premium each time she sells.
The research note says the STT increase on F&O may cut trading volumes.
terms.fill: Every contract note shows ____, the tax charged on the trade itself.
wrong: Tax on capital gains, paid when you file returns
GST charged on brokerage
Stamp duty paid to the state
terms.note: Rates change in Union Budgets, so check the latest before quoting a number.

terms.short: Official record of your day's trades
terms.definition: The legal document your broker sends after each trading day, listing your trades, prices, brokerage, taxes and other charges.
examples: Check the contract note for the exact charges.
Risk checks our trades against the broker's contract note every evening.
The client asked what the stamp duty line on her contract note means.
terms.fill: Your broker must send a ____ within 24 hours listing every trade and charge.
wrong: A futures contract
A notice from the exchange about price limits
A loan agreement for margin funding

terms.said: F P I (often still called F I I)
terms.short: Foreign investor in Indian markets
terms.definition: A foreign portfolio investor: an overseas fund or institution investing in Indian securities. Many people still use the older term FII.
examples: FIIs sold ₹5,000 crore in the cash market yesterday.
The analyst tracks FPI flows daily, because foreign money drives large caps in the short run.
Risk worries that heavy FPI selling could push the rupee lower.
terms.fill: Heavy selling by ____ often weakens both the market and the rupee.
wrong: An Indian mutual fund
A foreign company listed in India
An Indian investor living abroad
terms.note: An Indian living abroad is an NRI, not an FPI.

terms.short: Indian institutions such as MFs and insurers
terms.definition: Domestic institutional investors: Indian mutual funds, insurance companies, banks and pension funds. Their buying has often offset foreign selling in recent years.
examples: DIIs bought ₹3,000 crore as FIIs sold.
DII buying has cushioned the market every time foreigners sold this year.
The client asked who the DIIs are: mostly mutual funds and insurers such as LIC.
terms.fill: Indian mutual funds and LIC are counted as ____ in daily flow data.
wrong: Foreign funds investing in India
Individual investors trading online
Companies buying back their own shares

terms.short: Small individual investor
terms.definition: An individual investing small sums of their own money, as opposed to an institution or a wealthy investor. In Indian IPOs, the retail category covers individuals applying for up to ₹2 lakh.
examples: The retail portion was subscribed 20 times.
SEBI's study found that most retail investors in F&O lose money.
The broker's app is built for the retail investor, with small order sizes and simple screens.
terms.fill: A college student buying 10 shares through an app is a ____.
wrong: An investor in retail-sector stocks
Anyone who trades every day
A small company listed on the SME platform

terms.short: Wealthy individual investor
terms.definition: A high net worth individual. In Indian IPOs, individuals applying for more than ₹2 lakh fall in the non-institutional (NII) category, often called the HNI portion.
examples: HNI demand, from individuals bidding over ₹2 lakh each, drove the IPO's subscription.
The HNI portion of the IPO was subscribed 80 times, much of it with borrowed money.
The PMS is aimed at HNI clients who can invest ₹50 lakh or more.
terms.fill: An individual applying for ₹10 lakh of shares in an IPO bids in the ____ portion.
wrong: A highly leveraged trader
A foreign institution
An employee who gets stock options

terms.short: Pooled fund run by an AMC
terms.definition: A fund that pools money from many investors and invests it under a stated mandate. It is run by an asset management company and regulated by SEBI.
examples: Mutual funds now own a record share of Indian equities.
The client's mutual fund charges 0.5% a year in its direct plan.
The analyst says steady SIP money flowing into mutual fund schemes is why mid caps stay expensive.
terms.fill: Rather than pick stocks herself, she buys units of an equity ____ run by an AMC.
wrong: A loan shared between two banks
A savings account with a fixed rate
A company's employee pension plan

terms.short: Fixed regular investment into a fund
terms.definition: A systematic investment plan: investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually monthly. Monthly SIP inflows are a major support for Indian markets.
examples: Steady SIP flows give funds money to buy every month, even in a sell-off.
Monthly SIP inflows into equity funds are now above ₹20,000 crore.
The client asked whether to stop her SIP in a fall; the adviser said that's when it buys cheapest.
terms.fill: Putting ₹10,000 into a fund automatically every month is called a ____.
wrong: A one-time lump-sum investment
A plan to sell shares slowly
An insurance product with market returns
terms.note: People say both "sip" and "S I P".

terms.short: Per-unit value of a fund
terms.definition: Net asset value: a fund's assets minus its liabilities, divided by the number of units. Mutual fund units are bought and sold at the day's NAV.
examples: The fund's NAV rose 1.5% today.
Mutual fund orders placed before the cut-off time get that day's NAV.
The ETF trades close to its NAV because market makers trade away any gap.
terms.fill: You buy mutual fund units at that day's ____, not at a live market price.
wrong: The yearly fee a fund charges
The fund's total assets in rupees
The return promised by the fund

terms.short: Company that runs mutual funds
terms.definition: An asset management company: the firm that manages mutual fund schemes, such as SBI Mutual Fund or HDFC AMC.
examples: Listed AMCs rally when SIP flows rise.
The AMC launched a new Nifty index fund with a very low fee.
The analyst values the AMC on the money it manages and the fees it earns.
terms.fill: The fund manager works for an ____, which earns fees on the assets it manages.
wrong: A credit rating agency for funds
A broker that executes fund orders
The regulator for mutual funds
terms.note: On a demat statement, AMC can also mean annual maintenance charge.

terms.short: Promoter shares used as loan collateral
terms.definition: Shares that promoters have pledged as collateral for loans. High pledging is a warning sign, because a price fall can trigger forced selling by lenders.
examples: Promoter pledge rose to 40%, and the stock was hammered.
Risk avoids stocks with a high promoter pledge, because forced selling can crash them.
The client asked why promoter pledge matters: if the price falls, lenders can sell the shares.
terms.fill: When a stock falls, lenders may sell shares held under a ____, pushing the price down further.
wrong: A promise by promoters not to sell
A promoter's commitment to buy more shares
A donation by promoters to charity

tf.s: A sharp fall in the share price can force pledged promoter shares to be sold.
tf.why: Lenders sell pledged shares when their value drops below the loan's cover.

terms.short: Maximum daily price move for a stock
terms.definition: The most a stock's price can move in a day, set by the exchange as a price band such as 5%, 10% or 20%. Stocks in F&O have no fixed band and use dynamic limits instead.
examples: The exchange cut the band to 5% after wild moves.
The client couldn't sell because the stock hit its circuit limit early in the day.
Risk watches stocks near their circuit limit, because positions there may not be exitable.
terms.fill: The exchange cut the stock's ____ from 20% to 5% after wild moves.
wrong: The total shares a person may buy in a day
A rule that halts the whole market
The trading hours of the exchange

calcs.q: A stock closed at ₹200 and has a 5% price band. What is the highest price it can trade at today?
calcs.why: 5% of ₹200 is ₹10, so the upper limit is ₹210.

terms.short: Stuck at the maximum daily rise
terms.definition: When a stock rises to the top of its price band and can't trade higher that day. Usually only buyers are left.
examples: The stock hit upper circuit on the order win, with lakhs of shares waiting to be bought.
The client's buy order didn't fill: the stock was locked at upper circuit with no sellers.
Risk flags stocks that hit upper circuit day after day on thin volume.
terms.fill: With only buyers and no sellers at the limit, the stock is locked in ____.
wrong: When a stock falls to its daily limit
The highest price in 52 weeks
When the whole market halts

tf.s: A stock stuck at its upper circuit has plenty of buyers but almost no sellers.

terms.short: Stuck at the maximum daily fall
terms.definition: When a stock falls to the bottom of its price band and can't trade lower that day. Usually only sellers are left, so holders may be unable to exit.
examples: It's been in lower circuit for three days; nobody can get out.
Risk marks a stock stuck at lower circuit well below its last price, since nobody can sell there.
The client panicked when her small cap hit lower circuit after the fraud news.
terms.fill: Bad news hit, and the stock was locked in ____ with no buyers.
wrong: When a stock hits its maximum daily rise
When a stock hits its 52-week low
When SEBI suspends trading in a stock

terms.short: Whole-market halt on a big index move
terms.definition: A halt across all equity and equity derivatives trading when the Nifty 50 or Sensex moves 10%, 15% or 20% in a day. How long the halt lasts depends on the level and the time of day.
examples: The last market-wide halts in India were in March 2020.
A 10% fall in the Nifty or Sensex triggers a market-wide circuit breaker and halts trading.
Risk's crash plan assumes the market-wide circuit breaker could freeze the whole book for a while.
terms.fill: If the Sensex falls 10% in a day, a ____ halts trading across the market.
wrong: A limit on a single stock's daily move
A rule stopping foreign investors from selling
A power cut at the exchange

terms.short: Exchange watchlist with stricter rules
terms.definition: Additional Surveillance Measure: an exchange framework that puts stocks with unusual price or volume moves under stricter rules, such as 100% margin or tighter price bands.
examples: The stock moved into ASM stage 2, so traders now need full margin.
The client asked why her broker wants full margin on a stock: it's on the ASM list.
Risk checks the ASM list each morning before taking intraday positions.
terms.fill: After a 300% rally in two months, the exchanges put the stock under ____.
wrong: A SEBI ban on a company's promoters
An automatic sell mode for margin calls
The list of stocks eligible for F&O

terms.short: 9:00–9:15 am auction before trading
terms.definition: The session from 9:00 to 9:15 am, before normal trading, where orders are collected and a single opening price is found by call auction.
examples: The stock was indicated 8% higher in pre-open after the results.
The desk watches the pre-open price to see where the heavyweights will start the day.
The client's order placed at 9:05 was matched in the pre-open session.
terms.fill: The opening price of Nifty stocks is discovered in the ____ before 9:15 am.
wrong: A session open only to institutions
After-hours trading at the closing price
Time when the exchange tests its systems
terms.note: Order entry runs for the first few minutes, then matching happens around 9:10 to 9:12 am.

terms.short: End-of-day auction that sets the close
terms.definition: A short auction after normal trading ends that sets the official closing price of stocks with F&O contracts. Orders are collected for a few minutes, then matched at the single price that trades the most shares.
examples: Index funds now buy in the closing auction to match the official close.
The desk sends its index rebalance orders into the closing auction to get the official close.
Risk prefers to exit big positions in the closing auction, when liquidity is deepest.
terms.fill: For an F&O stock, the official closing price now comes from the ____, not from the last trade.
wrong: A session where shares delisted from the exchange are sold
Trading at the closing price after the market shuts
An auction of shares a seller failed to deliver

tf.s: The closing auction applies to every listed stock.
tf.why: It started with stocks that have F&O contracts on both NSE and BSE. Other stocks still close the old way.

terms.note: It began on 3 August 2026. From 7 December 2026, normal trading in these stocks runs to 3:30 pm and the auction to 3:40 pm, and F&O trades until 3:45 pm.

terms.short: Special Diwali trading session
terms.definition: A short, symbolic trading session held on Diwali to mark the start of the new Samvat year.
examples: Volumes are light in Muhurat trading; it's mostly symbolic buying.
The client buys one stock every year in Muhurat trading, for luck.
Risk keeps positions small in Muhurat trading because the session is short and thin.
terms.fill: Many investors buy a few shares during ____ on Diwali for good luck.
wrong: Trading allowed only on auspicious days
A morning auction before the market opens
A trading ban during festivals

terms.short: One large trade in a special window
terms.definition: A single large trade, at least ₹25 crore, done in a separate block deal window before the open or in the afternoon.
examples: A promoter sold a 3% stake through a block deal this morning.
The PM bought ₹300 crore of the stock in a block deal at a 3% discount.
Block deal prices are watched closely because they show where big holders are willing to sell.
terms.fill: A fund selling ₹500 crore of shares to another fund in one trade would use a ____.
wrong: Total trades by one client above 0.5% of a company's shares in a day
A trade blocked by the exchange
A deal that locks shares for a year

terms.short: One client trading over 0.5% of shares in a day
terms.definition: When one client's total trades in a stock during a day exceed 0.5% of the company's listed shares. Exchanges publish bulk deals every day.
examples: Bulk deal data shows a foreign fund bought 1.2% of the company.
The analyst checks bulk deal data every evening to see which funds are buying.
The client asked how a famous investor's purchase became news: it showed up as a bulk deal.
terms.fill: Exchanges disclose a ____ when one buyer trades more than 0.5% of a company's shares in a day.
wrong: A single trade of at least ₹25 crore in a special window
Buying shares in large lot sizes
A discount for trading many stocks together

terms.short: A company's first share sale to the public
terms.definition: An initial public offering: when a company first sells shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.
examples: The IPO was subscribed 50 times.
The analyst's IPO note says the price leaves little upside for long-term investors.
The client asked how IPO allotment works when retail demand is huge: lots are given out by lottery.
terms.fill: The startup raised ₹2,000 crore and listed on NSE through an ____.
wrong: A listed company's later share sale
A government bond auction
A share sale only to big institutions

terms.short: Unofficial premium before listing
terms.definition: Grey market premium: the unofficial premium at which IPO shares change hands before they list. It is unregulated and often unreliable.
examples: GMP was ₹200, but the stock listed flat.
The analyst warned clients not to trust GMP; it's an unregulated market.
GMP collapsed the day before listing when the market fell.
terms.fill: Before listing, traders watch the unofficial ____ to guess the listing price.
wrong: An official premium set by SEBI
The fee paid to IPO bankers
Gross margin percentage

terms.short: Profit on an IPO's first trading day
terms.definition: The profit from selling IPO shares on listing day, when the listing price is above the issue price.
examples: Most applicants were in it for listing gains.
The client sold on day one to lock in listing gains of 30%.
Risk notes that listing gains have shrunk as more IPOs crowd the market.
terms.fill: She bought IPO shares at ₹300 and sold them on the first day at ₹420, booking 40% ____.
wrong: Gains on shares held for over a year
Fees the exchange earns on a new listing
The rise in market cap over the first year

terms.short: Existing holders sell their shares
terms.definition: An offer for sale: existing shareholders such as promoters or the government sell their shares, in an IPO or through a special exchange window. The company gets no new money.
examples: The government sold 5% through an OFS.
The promoter will sell 2% through an OFS on Thursday, with retail bidding on Friday.
The client asked how to bid in the OFS: through her broker, much like a normal order.
terms.fill: When the government sells existing shares through a special exchange window with a separate retail day, it is an ____.
wrong: The company issues new shares to raise money
A discount offer for retail investors only
An offer by the company to buy back shares

terms.short: Quick share sale to institutions
terms.definition: A qualified institutional placement: a listed company raises money by selling new shares only to large institutions, usually at a small discount.
examples: The bank raised ₹5,000 crore through a QIP.
The stock fell 4% because the QIP was priced at a discount to the market.
The analyst says the QIP money will cut the company's debt by half.
terms.fill: Listed companies use a ____ to raise money quickly from institutions without a full public offer.
wrong: New shares offered to all existing shareholders in proportion
A listing on a foreign exchange
A sale of shares by promoters

terms.short: New shares offered to existing holders
terms.definition: An offer of new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, usually at a discount to the market price.
examples: A 1-for-5 rights issue at ₹400 a share.
The client must take up the rights issue or sell her entitlements, or her stake gets diluted.
The analyst says the deep discount in the rights issue is why the share price dropped.
terms.fill: To raise money while letting current shareholders keep their stake, the company announced a ____.
wrong: Free shares given to existing holders
A share sale only to institutions
Shares given to employees

terms.short: Free extra shares for holders
terms.definition: Free extra shares given to existing shareholders out of the company's reserves, such as 1 bonus share for every share held. The price adjusts down, so the value of your holding doesn't change.
examples: After the 1:1 bonus, the share price halved.
The client's holding doubled from 100 to 200 shares after the bonus issue.
Risk adjusts every stop and price history after a bonus issue.
terms.fill: In a 1:1 ____, you get one extra free share for each share you own.
wrong: New shares sold to holders at a discount
A special dividend paid in cash
Shares given to promoters as a reward

calcs.q: You own 100 shares at ₹600. After a 1:1 bonus, what do you hold?
calcs.why: The share count doubles and the price roughly halves, so the holding is still worth about ₹60,000.

tf.s: A 1:1 bonus issue gives you one extra share for every share you hold.

terms.short: Each share divided into smaller ones
terms.definition: Dividing each share into several shares with a lower face value, such as one ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares. The price falls in proportion, so value doesn't change.
examples: The ₹10 shares were split into ₹1 shares to improve liquidity.
The client asked if the stock split made her richer; it didn't, she just holds more, cheaper shares.
The analyst expects more small investors to buy after the stock split.
terms.fill: After a 1-to-5 ____, a ₹5,000 share trades around ₹1,000.
wrong: Splitting a company into two after a demerger
Free shares issued from reserves
A promoter selling half their shares
terms.note: A bonus issue comes out of reserves; a split only changes the face value.

calcs.q: You hold 50 shares at ₹2,000. The stock splits from ₹10 to ₹2 face value. What do you hold now?
calcs.why: Face value ÷ 5 means 5 times the shares at a fifth of the price.

tf.s: A stock split makes your holding worth more.
tf.why: You get more shares at a lower price; the total value stays the same.

terms.short: Date that decides who gets a payout
terms.definition: The date on which a company checks its register to decide which shareholders get a dividend, bonus or rights. Under T+1 you must buy at least one trading day before it.
examples: Record date for the dividend is Friday, so buy by Thursday.
The analyst noted the record date for the buyback, since only holders on that day can tender.
The client sold on the record date and still got the dividend, because her sale settled the next day.
terms.fill: To get the dividend, your name must be on the company's register on the ____.
wrong: The date the dividend is paid
The date the company announces results
The day a stock hits its all-time high

terms.short: Company buys its own shares
terms.definition: When a company buys its own shares from shareholders, returning cash and reducing the number of shares.
examples: The company announced a buyback at a 20% premium to the market price.
The analyst likes the buyback because the company has spare cash and few places to invest it.
The client asked whether to tender her shares in the buyback or just sell in the market.
terms.fill: Instead of paying a dividend, the company returned cash through a ____, cutting the number of shares.
wrong: A company buying another company
Promoters buying shares in the open market
Traders buying back shares they shorted

terms.short: A company event that changes its shares
terms.definition: Any event a company decides that changes its shares or pays its holders: dividends, bonus issues, splits, rights issues, buybacks, mergers and demergers. The exchange adjusts prices on the ex-date, and F&O contracts are adjusted so traders aren't helped or hurt by it. Backtests need prices adjusted for them.
examples: The 1:1 bonus is a corporate action, so the price halves on the ex-date.
Our backtest broke on a stock split because the prices weren't adjusted for corporate actions.
The exchange adjusted the futures lot size after the corporate action.
terms.fill: A bonus issue, a split or a dividend is a ____.
wrong: A trade by the company's promoters
A change in the company's credit rating
An order placed by a large institution

terms.short: Tax on equity gains held a year or less
terms.definition: Short-term capital gains: profit on listed shares or equity funds sold within 12 months of buying. Taxed at 20% for sales from 23 July 2024 (15% before that).
examples: Selling within the year turned the profit into STCG at 20%.
He waited two more weeks to avoid STCG.
STCG from F&O doesn't exist: F&O profits are business income.
terms.fill: Profit on shares sold eight months after buying is taxed as ____.
wrong: Tax on profit from shares held more than 12 months
Tax charged on every share trade, profit or not
Tax on dividends received

calcs.q: You make ₹50,000 profit on shares held 6 months. At 20%, what is the STCG tax?
calcs.why: Held under 12 months, so STCG at 20%: 0.2 × 50,000 = 10,000.

tf.s: Shares sold 11 months after buying count as short-term.
tf.why: Listed shares held 12 months or less are short-term.

terms.short: Tax on equity gains held over a year
terms.definition: Long-term capital gains: profit on listed shares or equity funds held more than 12 months. The first ₹1.25 lakh of such gains each year is tax-free; the rest is taxed at 12.5% for sales from 23 July 2024.
examples: She books ₹1.25 lakh of LTCG each March to use the yearly exemption.
Holding past one year turned the gain into LTCG at 12.5%.
The budget raised LTCG on equity from 10% to 12.5%.
terms.fill: Profit on shares held for two years, above the yearly ₹1.25 lakh exemption, is taxed as ____ at 12.5%.
wrong: Tax on profit from shares held 12 months or less
Tax on every rupee of share profit, with no exemption
Tax charged at the time you buy shares

calcs.q: You book ₹3,25,000 of long-term equity gains in a year. With a ₹1.25 lakh exemption and 12.5% tax, what do you pay?

tf.s: All long-term equity gains are taxed from the first rupee.
tf.why: The first ₹1.25 lakh a year is exempt; only the excess is taxed at 12.5%.

terms.short: First day a buyer misses the dividend
terms.definition: The first trading day on which a buyer of the share no longer gets the declared dividend, bonus or split. Under T+1 it is the same day as the record date, and the price usually drops by roughly the dividend that morning.
examples: The stock opened ₹12 lower because it went ex-date on its ₹12 dividend.
Buy before the ex-date if you want the dividend.
Under T+1, ex-date and record date fall on the same day.
terms.fill: Buy the share on its ____ and you don't get the dividend; buy the day before and you do.
wrong: The day the dividend is paid into your bank
The day the board announces the dividend
The last day you can sell and still get the dividend

tf.s: Buying a share on its ex-date still gets you the dividend.
tf.why: Ex-date is the first day buyers miss out. You must buy before it.

terms.short: Identity checks before you can invest
terms.definition: Know Your Customer: the identity and address checks (PAN, Aadhaar, address proof, a photo) that a broker, bank or fund house must complete before you can invest. Done once through a KYC registration agency, it is reused across firms.
examples: Her demat account opened in a day because her KYC was already registered.
The fund froze new SIPs until his KYC was updated.
Brokers can't take orders from you until KYC is done.
terms.fill: Before a broker can open your account, it must complete ____ checks on your PAN and address.
wrong: The broker's check that you have enough margin
The exchange's check that an order is within price bands
A tax form filed each year

tf.s: You must redo full KYC with every new broker or fund house.
tf.why: KYC is registered once with a KYC registration agency and other firms can fetch it.

terms.short: 12-character ID code for a security
terms.definition: International Securities Identification Number: a 12-character code that identifies one security worldwide. Indian ones start "IN". Unlike a ticker, it doesn't change between exchanges.
examples: Check the ISIN, not the name; two bonds of the same company look alike.
Reliance has one ISIN even though it trades on NSE and BSE.
The depository tracks your holdings by ISIN.
terms.fill: A 12-character code starting "IN" that identifies the security itself, whatever exchange it trades on, is its ____.
wrong: The short symbol a stock trades under on NSE
Your demat account number
The code for a broker on the exchange

tf.s: A share listed on both NSE and BSE has one ISIN.
tf.why: The ISIN identifies the security, not the exchange.

terms.short: IPO money blocked, not debited, until allotment
terms.definition: Application Supported by Blocked Amount: the way you apply for an IPO in India. Your bank blocks the money in your account (often through a UPI mandate) and debits it only for the shares you are actually allotted.
examples: The ₹15,000 for the IPO is blocked under ASBA but still earns interest.
No allotment, so the ASBA block was released.
He approved the UPI mandate for ASBA on his phone.
terms.fill: When you apply for an IPO, the bank blocks your money instead of debiting it; this system is called ____.
wrong: The price at which IPO shares list
Shares set aside for big investors in an IPO
A loan to buy IPO shares

tf.s: Under ASBA, the full application money leaves your account the day you apply.
tf.why: It is only blocked; the bank debits it on allotment and releases the rest.

terms.short: Big institution allotted a day before the IPO
terms.definition: A large institutional investor allotted IPO shares one working day before the issue opens to the public. Their buying signals demand, and their shares come with a lock-in so they can't sell on listing day.
examples: The IPO raised ₹1,800 crore from anchor investors the day before it opened.
Watch the stock when the anchor investor lock-in ends.
Big mutual funds and FPIs showed up as anchor investors.
terms.fill: The institutions allotted IPO shares a day before the public offer opens, under a lock-in, are each called an ____.
wrong: A promoter who keeps most of the shares
A retail investor who applies for the maximum lot
The bank that manages the IPO

tf.s: Anchor investors can sell their IPO shares on listing day.
tf.why: Anchor shares are locked in for a period after allotment.

terms.short: Listed trust owning rent-paying property
terms.definition: Real Estate Investment Trust: a listed trust that owns income-producing property, such as offices and malls, and must pay out most of its income to unitholders. Its units trade on the exchange like shares.
examples: The office REIT yields about 7% from rent.
REIT units dropped when office occupancy fell.
A REIT lets you own a slice of offices without buying a building.
terms.fill: A listed trust that owns office parks and pays out most of the rent to unitholders is a ____.
wrong: A trust that owns roads and power lines
A home loan company
A fund that buys shares of real estate developers

tf.s: A REIT must pass most of its income to unitholders.
tf.why: That payout rule is what makes REITs an income product.

terms.short: Listed trust owning infrastructure
terms.definition: Infrastructure Investment Trust: a listed trust that owns income-earning infrastructure such as toll roads, power transmission lines or gas pipelines, and pays out most of its cash flow to unitholders.
examples: The InvIT owns twelve toll roads and pays out quarterly.
Power-grid InvITs are popular for their steady payouts.
InvIT units fall when bond yields rise, much like bonds.
terms.fill: A listed trust that owns toll roads and pays out most of its cash to unitholders is an ____.
wrong: A trust that owns offices and malls
A fund that lends to infrastructure firms
A government bond for infrastructure

tf.s: An InvIT owns offices and malls.
tf.why: That's a REIT. An InvIT owns infrastructure like roads, power lines and pipelines.

terms.short: Yearly return with uneven cash flows
terms.definition: The annualised return on investments made and withdrawn on different dates, such as SIP instalments. It weights each cash flow by how long it was invested, so it is the fair way to measure SIP returns. CAGR fits only a single lump sum.
examples: Your SIP's XIRR is 14%, even though the fund's 5-year CAGR is 16%.
Use XIRR, not absolute return, to compare SIPs.
The app shows XIRR because you invested on 36 different dates.
terms.fill: For a SIP with 36 monthly instalments, the right yearly return figure is the ____, not CAGR.
wrong: The return on a single lump sum held for several years
The total percentage gain, ignoring time
A fund's return compared with its benchmark

tf.s: CAGR is the right measure for a SIP with many monthly instalments.
tf.why: CAGR assumes one lump sum. A SIP's dated cash flows need XIRR.

terms.short: The broker's fee for each trade
terms.definition: The fee a stockbroker charges for executing a trade. Discount brokers usually charge a flat fee per order, often ₹20 or less, and some charge nothing on delivery buys. Full-service brokers charge a percentage of the trade value and add research and advice. It is one line on the contract note, next to STT, exchange charges, stamp duty and GST.
examples: Brokerage was only ₹40 for the round trip, but STT and other charges added ₹300 more.
Full-service brokerage at 0.3% of value adds up fast for an active trader.
GST is charged on brokerage, not on the trade value.
terms.fill: The fee your stockbroker charges you for placing a trade is ____.
wrong: The tax collected on each trade
The interest charged on margin funding
The fee the exchange charges for listing

terms.short: Low-cost online broker, no advice
terms.definition: A broker that charges low flat fees per order and offers an app and platform but no personal advice or research. Discount brokers now hold most of India's active retail clients. The trade-off is that you make every call yourself.
examples: Switching to a discount broker cut her brokerage from 0.3% to ₹20 an order.
Most new F&O traders open accounts with a discount broker.
A discount broker won't call you with a stock tip; a full-service one might.
terms.fill: A broker charging a flat ₹20 an order with no research or advice is a ____.
wrong: A broker who trades with the firm's own money
A broker that only deals in mutual funds
A dealer who gives clients a discount on IPOs

terms.short: Tax on the buyer's side of each trade
terms.definition: A tax on transferring securities, charged only on the buyer's side of each trade at a single national rate and collected by the exchange or depository for the states. The rate is small but differs by segment: highest on delivery buys, lower on intraday, futures and options.
examples: The contract note showed stamp duty only on the buy leg.
Stamp duty on delivery buys is higher than on intraday trades.
Since 2020 stamp duty on trades is one rate across India, not set state by state.
terms.fill: The small tax charged only on the buy side of every trade, collected for the states, is ____.
wrong: Tax on capital gains when you sell
GST charged on brokerage
A fee the exchange charges every member
terms.note: Rates are set by law and can change, so check the current rate before quoting a number.

tf.s: Stamp duty on a share trade is charged to both the buyer and the seller.
tf.why: Only the buyer pays stamp duty. STT, by contrast, can apply to both sides depending on the segment.
